newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia must create jobs via infrastructure - Lopez.
newsitem.headline: Colombia must create jobs via infrastructure - Lopez.

text.p: BOGOTA, May 7 Reuter - Colombia should dedicate more resources to infrastructure projects in a bid to rein in growing unemployment, National Planning Department head Cecilia Lopez said Wednesday.

Lopez admitted that President Ernesto Samper's administration was falling far short of its goal of creating 1.6 million new jobs over four years and said that even a return to more vigorous economic growth would not necessarily generate much-needed jobs.
"In terms of the number of jobs, we're far short of our goal and the bad news is that the reactivation of the economy will not necessarily generate the jobs we need," Lopez told a press conference.
"If we put resources into infrastructure, then we can kill several birds with one stone. We could create between 14,000 and 15,000 new jobs," she added.
Colombia's urban unemployment rate was running at 12.7 percent in the first quarter of this year -- the highest level in nine years -- up from 11.3 percent at the end of 1996.

Lopez said part of that rise was due to the sharp slowdown in the economy. Gross domestic product GDP grew just 2.1 percent in 1996 -- one of the lowest rates in decades. For this year, Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo forecasts GDP growth of about 4 percent.
The independent National Association of Financial Institutions ANIF sees lower growth and last week warned the urban unemployment rate could peak at about 14 percent by mid- year.

In Wednesday's press conference, Lopez said infrastructure programs had been one of the most effective areas of government spending since Samper took office in 1994. She added that continued high spending was necessary in order to modernize Colombia's transport and communications network and make it more competitive in the international market place.

Infrastructure investment for Samper's four-year term of office is forecast to hit 25 trillion pesos by August 1998, equivalent to about 5.6 percent of GDP, excluding investment in the mining and oil sector, Lopez said.

In the last two years, private sector investment in infrastructure projects had increased fourfold to levels equivalent to about 1.6 percent of GDP, according to National planning Department figures. Lopez said this was one of the highest levels of private sector participation in infrastructure in Latin America.
